beats.intro: Chapter five, lesson two. Nucleic acids, from gene to protein. [[recipe]]A cook follows a recipe, and the cake is the result. [[cell]]A cell works the same way. [[dna]]Its recipes are written in DNA, and its dishes are proteins. [[ask]]How does a recipe in DNA become a protein?
beats.gene: Zoom into a cell. [[nucleus]]Near its center sits the nucleus, and inside it, the DNA. [[gene]]A short stretch of DNA that holds one recipe is called a gene. [[poly]]The recipe is for a polypeptide, a chain of amino acids. [[prog]]So the order of amino acids in a polypeptide is programmed by a gene. [[made]]And genes are made of DNA, which is a nucleic acid.
beats.scale: A gene is only a small part of the story. [[mol]]One DNA molecule is a single, very long double helix. [[chrom]]In a cell, each long molecule is wound up with proteins into a package called a chromosome. [[genes]]One chromosome carries many genes, a little like chapters in a long book. [[between]]A gene is just one short stretch. The DNA between genes is not a recipe for a polypeptide.
beats.roles: There are two kinds of nucleic acid. [[dna]]Deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA. [[rna]]And ribonucleic acid, or RNA. [[rep]]DNA gives directions for its own replication. Before a cell divides, it copies its DNA, so each new cell gets a full set of recipes. [[mrna]]DNA also directs the making of messenger RNA, called mRNA, and through mRNA, it controls protein synthesis. [[why]]The messenger is a working copy. The master recipe stays safe in the nucleus.
beats.compare: Now put the two nucleic acids side by side. [[sugar]]Their sugars differ. DNA has deoxyribose, and RNA has ribose. [[base]]Both use A, G, and C. But DNA uses T, thymine, where RNA uses U, uracil. [[strand]]DNA is usually double-stranded, two chains wound together. RNA is usually a single strand. [[where]]DNA stays in the nucleus. RNA is found in the nucleus, and out in the cytoplasm too. [[job]]DNA stores the genetic information. RNA takes part in using it.
beats.why: Why make a copy at all? [[one]]A cell has one master set of DNA, and it has to last. [[risk]]Sending it into the busy cytoplasm would risk damaging it. [[many]]A copy is cheap. One gene can give many mRNA strands, and each one can be read by a ribosome, again and again. [[fade]]And mRNA does not last long. When a cell stops making copies of a gene, the supply fades, so the cell can change which proteins it makes.
beats.q2: Quick check. Sort the facts about DNA and RNA.
beats.flow: Follow one recipe from gene to protein. [[one]]Step one. In the nucleus, DNA directs the synthesis of an mRNA strand. [[pore]]Step two. The mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore, and moves into the cytoplasm. [[ribo]]Step three. In the cytoplasm, the mRNA meets a ribosome. [[aa]]Amino acids float nearby. [[chain]]The ribosome uses the mRNA to string amino acids into a polypeptide, one after another. [[name]]That is protein synthesis, and it happens at ribosomes. [[all]]So the order is DNA, then mRNA, then protein.
beats.example: Let's walk through one example. Take insulin, a protein made by cells in the pancreas. [[gene]]The insulin gene is a stretch of DNA in the nucleus. [[copy]]When the cell needs insulin, it makes an mRNA copy of that gene. [[out]]The mRNA slips out through a nuclear pore into the cytoplasm. [[read]]There, a ribosome reads the mRNA, and adds amino acids one at a time. [[fold]]The finished polypeptide then folds up and works as a protein. [[same]]Cells elsewhere in the body hold the same insulin gene, but they do not make this mRNA, so they do not make the protein.
beats.q1: Quick check. Where does each step happen?
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]A gene is a unit of inheritance, made of DNA, that programs the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide. [[w2]]There are two nucleic acids, DNA and RNA. DNA directs its own replication, and the making of mRNA. [[w3]]mRNA carries the message out through a nuclear pore. [[w4]]Ribosomes read it and build the polypeptide. [[end]]Now try the practice.
